output.brief: The evidence points to the cut in merit awards, not the Admissions Office, as the main cause of the drop. Yield fell only in the Dean's tier (45.2% to 31.9%) and the Merit tier (44.9% to 32.3%), where awards were cut from $14,000 to $9,000 and from $9,000 to $5,000. It was flat in the Presidential tier, where awards were unchanged, and nearly flat among students with no merit award. Applications, admits and GPA all rose, so a weaker applicant pool is not the explanation. Early-action students had their decisions on the old timetable and old system. Their yield still fell by about the same amount (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular decision (39.0% to 31.5%). So the late regular-decision answers were not the main driver, though they did hurt some individual students. Regular decision was probably a smaller contributor, and I can't size it. I'm fairly confident, but this is not a controlled test. Next steps: don't replace the director on this basis. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly turnaround target for regular decision. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-transcript claims are checked.
